name: Great Barrier Reef
blurb: Corals, grazers and sharks, and what happens when the starfish boom.

tip.title: Try a starfish outbreak
tip.text: Crown-of-thorns starfish eat coral. Raise them by 200% to see an outbreak spread, then raise the giant triton that eats them.

nodes.desc: Tiny drifting animals that graze phytoplankton and feed fish, manta rays and coral.
Grazes seagrass meadows, which keeps them healthy.
Eats coral polyps. Outbreaks can strip large stretches of reef.
Winter visitors that feed on small animals among reef-flat algae and rubble before flying north to breed in the Arctic.
Eats turtles, dugongs, fish and carrion, and roams widely over seagrass and reef.

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Great Barrier Reef). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.
story: The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system, over 2,900 reefs off Queensland built by billions of coral polyps. Parrotfish and surgeonfish graze its algae, turtles and dugongs graze seagrass, and crown-of-thorns starfish eat coral.
matters: The reef has lost more than half its coral cover since 1985. Bleaching and starfish outbreaks did the damage, but fast-growing Acropora coral drove the strongest recovery in 36 years in 2022.
